edges.effect_quant: School-based interventions tend to produce small average child-health gains: a meta-analysis of adolescent BMI programs found a pooled BMI z-score improvement of -0.06 (95% CI -0.10 to -0.03), a meta-analysis of accelerometer-based school programs found lower sedentary time (g=-0.08, 95% CI -0.12 to -0.03) but no overall MVPA gain, and a middle-school nutrition and exercise trial reduced BMI percentile among students who were obese at baseline by 2.33 percentile points.
edges.population: children and adolescents exposed to structured school-based health interventions
edges.mechanism: Schools can influence child health through repeated exposure, peer norms, staff reinforcement, environmental changes, and curriculum-linked behavior practice. Those levers usually create modest average improvements rather than dramatic ones, but they can still matter at population scale and may be stronger in higher-risk subgroups.
edges.summary: The overall direction is positive but modest. School-based health interventions can improve some child outcomes, especially BMI trajectory, sedentary time, and selected diet or activity patterns, although average effects are usually small and not every trial shows a broad benefit across all endpoints.
edges.caveats: This edge combines different child outcomes, including anthropometric and activity-related measures, so some inconsistency is expected. Interventions seem most successful when they are multi-component and modify both the school environment and student behavior rather than relying on brief health education alone.

evidence.citation: Jacob CM et al 2021 Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act
evidence.notes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of school-based interventions with health education to reduce body mass index in adolescents aged 10 to 19 years.
